concepts.objective: Distinguish an observed association from the effect of deliberately changing a variable.

sources.citation: Peters, Jonas; Janzing, Dominik; Schölkopf, Bernhard. Elements of Causal Inference: Foundations and Learning Algorithms. MIT Press, 2017.

claims.proposition: An observed association describes how variables vary together in an observational distribution.

source_refs.locator: Section 1.4.1, Model (i), paragraph defining the observational distribution

claims.proposition: Different causal models can produce the same observational distribution while implying different intervention distributions; without additional causal assumptions or interventional evidence, observation alone may not identify an intervention effect.
Observing a variable at a value and intervening to set it to that value can produce different distributions.

resources.text: A dataset shows that people who sleep longer report better concentration. Which conclusion is justified by this observation alone?
Ask whether observing people with different sleep durations is the same as assigning a different sleep duration.

An observed association describes how variables vary together. Without additional causal assumptions or interventional evidence, it does not by itself determine what would happen under an intervention.
Yes. The observation supports an association, but without additional causal assumptions or interventional evidence, it does not by itself identify what would happen if sleep were assigned.
That conclusion treats an observed difference as an intervention effect. Different causal models can match the same observational pattern while implying different intervention outcomes.

choices.text: Longer sleep is associated with better reported concentration, but the observation alone does not identify the effect of making someone sleep longer.
Making any person sleep longer will improve that person's concentration.
